speaker: Doctor
text: Welcome to your consultation. I understand you have knee pain after recently increasing your physical activity; to help me identify the specific cause, can you describe exactly where the pain is located and what movements make it worse?

speaker: Patient
text: 23-year-old female. The patient presents with knee pain that started yesterday and has been steadily worsening. She cites recent participation in volleyball involving repetitive pivoting and twisting movements as a possible cause. She was advised at her last physical exam that weight loss could be beneficial for her health.

speaker: Doctor
text:
Thank you for the details. Given the history of pivoting and twisting movements during volleyball, I need to determine if there is joint instability or a specific mechanical block. Did you hear a loud "pop" at the time of injury, and do you currently feel your knee giving way or buckling when you try to stand?

speaker: Doctor
text: Based on the MRI results showing normal anatomy and your description of the "pop" with instability, a complete ACL tear seems unlikely; instead, this presentation is highly suggestive of a Meniscal Tear or a Grade 1 MCL sprain. To confirm which structure is injured, does the pain specifically worsen when you rotate your knee while it is bent, or does it hurt more when you apply direct pressure to the inner or outer joint line?

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Knee pain, specifically over the medial aspect of the tibia just inferior to the patella. I also have Recent weight loss attempt, Increased physical activity.

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Insall-Salvati Ratio Abnormality (Patellar Tendonitis) / Osgood-Schlatter Disease. The patient's pain localized to the medial aspect of the tibia inferior to the patella, combined with recent increased physical activity and weight loss attempts, is characteristic of patellar tendon pathology or enthesopathy rather than an ACL tear or meniscal injury.
